summary: The seam, the record and the fake are the right shape and the per-stream offset behaviour is real (verified: making offsets global fails exactly the 2 tests the row claims). One major: the stated contract promises an at-most-once/idempotent retry and says an IOException means 'the commit did not happen' -- neither is true of anything in this tree (M4.10 is todo, the fake explicitly does not model it) and neither is supported by the store SPI, whose IOException is 'unreachable', i.e. ambiguous. The claim appears in four places.

findings.title: The contract promises at-most-once retry and a definite 'did not happen' on IOException; the tree provides neither and the SPI does not support the second
findings.detail: Three assertions, all unsupported. (a) ':33-34' -- 'only that each [flushSeq] is applied at most once'; (b) ':36-39' -- 'IOException means the commit did not happen and may be retried with the SAME (podId, flushSeq) -- that pair is the idempotency key precisely so a retry after an ambiguous failure cannot assign a second set of offsets'; (c) ':58-59' -- '@throws IOException the commit did not happen'. Nothing in the tree implements idempotency on (podId, flushSeq): M4.10 is 'todo' and FakeSequencer.java:27 says the fake does not model it 'for now'. And BinStore.java:32-36 defines IOException as 'the store is unreachable', which is exactly the ambiguous case -- a conditional PUT whose response is lost has landed. The sentence contradicts itself: 'the commit did not happen' and 'a retry after an ambiguous failure' cannot both be true. This is not a future-tense description; it is written as the property a caller may rely on today, and M4.2 lands a real implementation two rows from now.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.2 wires the CommitLog-backed Sequencer and a caller (or a retry decorator, or a simulation seed at M4.12) follows this javadoc: on IOException it re-submits the same CommitRequest. The original putIfAbsent had in fact landed -- only the response was lost -- so the records are already committed at offsets [N, N+k). The retry redrives to the next free sequence and commits the same runs again at [M, M+k). Both deltas are durable and both are fanned out, so every consumer of that stream receives the records twice at two different offsets: the silent duplication M4.10's own backlog row says it exists to prevent. No test can catch it before M4.10, because the fake models no idempotency at all, so a retry test written against the fake passes while constraining nothing.
findings.suggested_fix: State the failure model as it is: an IOException leaves the outcome UNKNOWN; the retry is safe with the same (podId, flushSeq) ONCE M4.10 lands, and until then a retry may assign a second set of offsets. Same for ':33-34'. Note this claim has FOUR copies -- Sequencer.java:33-34, Sequencer.java:36-39, Sequencer.java:58-59 and the backlog row's '`IOException` means the commit did not happen' -- plus a fifth in FakeSequencerTest.java:117-120, whose assertion description ('flushSeq 0 from a DIFFERENT node is a different commit, not a replay') implies the fake distinguishes replays when it never dedups anything. M4.0's recurring defect was fixing one copy of a fact and missing its duplicates.

findings.title: The '-'/'/' guard is justified by a key grammar that does not exist for this field, and the field name diverges from the established podShortId
findings.detail: The stated reason is 'they are separators in the key grammar, so a podId carrying one yields a key that parses back to something else'. That is SegmentKey's reason (SegmentKey.java:71-83 and :177-206: the header-length marker is matched inside the substring after the key's last '/', so a hyphen in podShortId can produce a spurious match). No sequencer key contains podId: M4.0 settled the chain path as ctl/log/<slot>/<epoch>/<seq>.delta specifically against the <podId> form, and M4.8's per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq lives in a checkpoint BODY. So the comment asserts a key that does not exist. The guard is defensible only if podId is by definition the same value SegmentPublisher.java:51-67 and SegmentKey already constrain -- but that value is called podShortId in both places, while this record calls it podId and documents it merely as 'which node produced this commit'.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.2/M5 wiring passes the node's Kubernetes pod name (the downward-API POD_NAME, which contains '-' in every StatefulSet and Deployment) because nothing in the record's name or javadoc says it must be the hyphen-free short id. Every commit then throws IllegalArgumentException on the ingest path at runtime rather than at startup. The mirror failure is quieter: a caller that satisfies the guard with some other hyphen-free id ends up with an idempotency-key identity that is not the identity in its own segment keys, so M4.10's per-pod state and the segments disagree about who the node is.
findings.suggested_fix: Either name it podShortId, matching SegmentKey and SegmentPublisher, or keep podId and say in the javadoc that it is the SAME identity SegmentPublisher takes -- and replace the 'key grammar' reason with the real one (it must round-trip through the segment key grammar / it is the fleet-wide node identity).

findings.title: Validation reads the caller's mutable map; the defensive copy is taken afterwards
findings.detail: Every guard (isEmpty, per-entry non-null and positive) runs against the map the caller handed in, and 'recordCounts = Map.copyOf(recordCounts)' happens last. The record's own comment says the copy exists because 'this record crosses a seam and, from M5, a network', i.e. the caller is not trusted to leave the map alone -- but the guards trust exactly that.
findings.failure_scenario: An accumulator that reuses its per-flush map mutates an entry to 0 (or removes the last entry) on another thread between the loop and the copy. The CommitRequest is then constructed carrying a zero count, and the failure surfaces later inside RunCommit's constructor ('a run with no records is not committed') deep in the sequencer -- precisely the 'several layers down' failure the comment at :53-59 says refusing at the seam avoids.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy first, then validate the copy: 'recordCounts = Map.copyOf(recordCounts);' before the isEmpty/entry loop (Map.copyOf already rejects null keys and values, so the requireNonNull on the entry key can go).

findings.title: Nothing sized by the sender is bounded, in a record whose javadoc says it crosses a network
findings.detail: security.md rule 5 -- 'Anything sized by client input has a bound. Frame lengths, batch counts, key lengths, queue depths.' The record advertises itself as shaped for a request arriving from another node from the first commit, and validates content but not size: podId length, segmentKey length and recordCounts cardinality are all unbounded.
findings.failure_scenario: At M5 a forwarded commit (from a peer, or from a peer that is confused rather than malicious) carries a multi-megabyte podId or a recordCounts map with millions of entries. The podId becomes a key in the per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq map M4.8 writes into every checkpoint, so one bad sender grows every checkpoint object without limit -- and M4.8's own row budgets the checkpoint at ~38 KiB.
findings.suggested_fix: Bound podId and segmentKey length (segmentKey against SegmentKey.MAX_KEY_BYTES, which already exists) and state where the recordCounts cardinality bound lives if it is deliberately the transport's job at M5.

findings.title: The return contract is written for an unbatched commit, and M4.7 batches
findings.detail: '@return the durable delta, carrying each run's assigned firstOffset' and 'the offsets in the returned CommitDelta are final' describe a one-request-one-delta world. M4.7 (two rows on) makes one delta carry 'every stream AND every contributing pod flush' in a commitBatchInterval window, and ADR-0001 rules out partition leadership, so two nodes can hold records for the same stream in the same window. The task's whole justification is that the shape must not change later; the request shape was reasoned about and the response shape was not.
findings.failure_scenario: At M4.7 a batched delta contains the runs of several requests. A caller receives a delta whose runs() include other nodes' runs and, when two nodes contributed to the same RunKey in one window, either two RunCommits with the same key or one merged RunCommit -- in both cases the caller cannot identify which offsets are its own. AC6's 'returns the original assignment' then forces either a return-type change or a re-reading of the contract so that the returned delta is a per-caller projection rather than 'the durable delta' -- the change this commit exists to avoid.
findings.suggested_fix: One sentence in the contract saying what the returned delta is when the implementation batches (the caller's own runs, projected; or the shared durable delta and the caller must locate its runs), so M4.7 is a fill-in rather than a contract revision.

findings.title: '428 tests green across all modules' -- measured 427
findings.detail: Ran ./gradlew test on the staged tree and summed tests= across every module's build/test-results/test/*.xml: binstore-backends 86, binstore-spi 29, client 15, format 122, http 36, ingest 93, plugin 34, sequencer 12 = 427, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped. The row's other measured claim checks out exactly: replacing FakeSequencer's per-stream offsets with a global counter fails 2 tests (eachStreamHasItsOwnOffsetSpace, partitionsOfTheSameIndexAreSeparateStreams), and the tree was restored afterwards with the staged hash unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: A number in a backlog row is the only durable record that a gate was run, and non-negotiable 4 makes it the thing every other rule rests on. A count that is off by one is indistinguishable from a count copied forward from an earlier run rather than measured, which is exactly the doubt the rule exists to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: State 427, or say what the 428th is (buildSrc's harness tests are a separate suite and are not 'all modules').
